name: BoolQ
description: A reading comprehension dataset of naturally occurring yes/no questions. Each example consists of a question, a paragraph from a Wikipedia article, the title of the article, and an answer, which is either "yes" or "no".
creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova
citeAs: Clark, Christopher and Lee, Kenton and Chang, Ming-Wei and Kwiatkowski, Tom and Collins, Michael and Toutanova, Kristina. BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions. arXiv:1905.10044v1, 2019.
rai:dataCollection: We gather data using the pipeline from Natural Questions (NQ), but with an additional filtering step to focus on yes/no questions. Questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine. Queries that are likely to be yes/no questions are heuristically identified by selecting queries where the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words and are of sufficient length. Questions are only kept if a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five results, in which case the question and Wikipedia page are given to a human annotator for further processing. Annotators label question/article pairs in a three-step process: first they decide if the question is good, meaning it is comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information; next, for good questions, annotators find a passage within the document that contains enough information to answer the question, and can mark questions as not answerable if the Wikipedia article does not contain the requested information; finally, annotators mark whether the question's answer is yes or no. The dataset combines 13k questions gathered from this pipeline with an additional 3k questions with yes/no answers from the NQ training set to reach a total of 16k questions.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, Document analysis, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine and Wikipedia pages/articles returned among the first five search results; additionally 3k questions with yes/no answers from the Natural Questions training set.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Unlike in NQ, the dataset only uses questions that were marked as having a yes/no answer, and pairs each question with the selected passage instead of the entire document. This was done to reduce ambiguity, avoid cases where the document supplies conflicting answers in different paragraphs, and keep the input small enough so that existing entailment models can easily be applied. The 16k questions were split into a 3.2k dev set, 3.2k test set, and 9.4k train set, ensuring questions from NQ are always in the train set.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Queries likely to be yes/no questions were heuristically identified by selecting queries whose first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words and that are of sufficient length. Questions were only kept if a Wikipedia page was returned as one of the first five results. Only questions marked as having a yes/no answer were retained, and each question was paired with the selected passage rather than the entire document.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators label question/article pairs in a three-step process. First, they decide if the question is good, meaning it is comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information; this judgment is made before the annotator sees the Wikipedia page. Next, for good questions, annotators find a passage within the document that contains enough information to answer the question; annotators can mark questions as not answerable if the Wikipedia article does not contain the requested information. Finally, annotators mark whether the question's answer is yes or no. For annotation quality assessment, three of the authors labeled 110 randomly chosen examples; if there was a disagreement, the authors conferred and selected a single answer by mutual agreement to create gold-standard labels.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: On 110 randomly chosen examples, the answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to gold-standard labels created by three authors. Of the cases where the answer annotation differed from the gold-standard, six were ambiguous or debatable cases, and five were errors where the annotator misunderstood the passage. Because agreement was sufficiently high, the authors elected to use singly-annotated examples in the training/dev/test sets in order to gather a larger dataset.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Three of the authors labeled 110 randomly chosen examples for annotation quality assessment.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper argues that naturally occurring yes/no questions have the benefit of being directly related to the practical end-task of answering user yes/no questions, and that using natural sources avoids optimizing models for an artificial setting without obvious end-use applications.
rai:dataBiases: Yes answers are slightly more common, with 62.31% in the train set. The paper also notes correlations between question topic/type and the likelihood of a yes answer, though these are too weak to outperform the majority baseline. Questions are gathered only when a Wikipedia page is among the first five Google search results, and the dataset uses naturally occurring search queries.
rai:dataLimitations: Annotating the data is expensive because annotators need to search entire Wikipedia documents for relevant evidence and read the text carefully. The dataset uses singly-annotated examples in the train/dev/test sets. Some annotation disagreements were due to ambiguous or debatable cases and annotator misunderstanding. The inference-type analysis may be slightly out-of-date because the dataset was updated after the analysis. The paper also suggests future work could build a document-level version of the task, which would increase difficulty and correspondence to an end-user application.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended as a reading comprehension benchmark for answering naturally occurring yes/no questions and for testing models' inferential abilities. It is split into a 9.4k train set, 3.2k dev set, and 3.2k test set.
